sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`database/sql` is Go's standard interface for relational databases. It gives applications common types for database handles, queries, rows, statements, and transactions, while a separate driver performs the database-specific network work.

An `*sql.DB` is a long-lived handle that manages a pool of underlying connections. `sql.Open` may only validate its arguments, so startup code normally calls `PingContext` when it must prove the database is reachable.

For example, a service can call `db.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, id).Scan(&user.Name)` to read one user. The context places a deadline on the call, and `Scan` makes the expected result shape explicit.

The package does not include a database driver, generate SQL, or map rows to structs automatically. Query text, argument placeholders, transaction boundaries, null handling, and connection limits remain application decisions.

Use `database/sql` when an application needs SQL with direct control over queries, scanning, transactions, timeouts, and pool settings. Create one shared `*sql.DB` for the process instead of opening a handle for every request.

sections.title: The core model: the database/sql package
sections.content:
the database/sql package is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The standard package separates the application's SQL workflow from the wire protocol used by PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, or another database. A driver registers itself, and the application opens a handle with the driver's name and its data-source settings. The handle is safe for concurrent use and obtains or reuses physical connections as work arrives. A query that returns rows owns resources until those rows are closed. A transaction temporarily binds its work to one connection so its statements share the same database session. This model explains several practical rules: keep the handle for the application's lifetime, configure pool limits deliberately, use placeholders for values, carry request cancellation through `Context`, and handle `NULL` with nullable Go types or SQL expressions. Errors are part of the data contract; no row, malformed SQL, a canceled deadline, and a lost connection do not mean the same thing.

sections.title: the database/sql package example
the database/sql package at a glance
sections.content:
| Value | Real meaning | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| `*sql.DB` || Concurrent handle and connection pool | Usually the whole process |
| `*sql.Conn` | One reserved connection | Close after the session work |
| `*sql.Tx` | Transaction bound to one connection | Until commit or rollback |
| `*sql.Rows` | Cursor over a result set | Until exhausted or closed |
